0509-value.caption: “Assessed Value of Household and Kitchen Furniture Owned by Georgia Negroes,” which employs the now-iconic Du Boisian spiral, combined with increasingly bright and saturated colors, to emphasize the increasing total value over time. 0509-value.altText: Six vertically stacked bars spiral toward the page’s center to show the value of Black Georgians’ household furniture. Each subsequent bar grows longer than the last, showing the increasing value of furniture Black Georgians owned from 1875 to 1899.
0509-value.altTextLong: A bar chart where six curving bars of color spiral toward the center of the page to indicate the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians from 1875 to 1899. The colors are all aligned in a row at the top of the page from 1875 to 1899, and each color corresponds to a year and value dollar amount. The topmost bar for 1875 is pink and is the smallest curving line, just barely beginning to curve, with the value of household furniture coming to $21,186. A blue curving bar falls just under the pink to represent 1880’s value of kitchen and household furniture, reaching $498,532. The next curving bar is brown for the year 1885 with a value of Black-owned furniture in Georgia reaching $736,170. Beneath the brown bar is a yellow curving bar for 1890, for which $1,173,624 was assessed to be the value of household and kitchen items owned by Black Georgians. The second bottom-most curving light gray bar shows that the value for Black-owned furniture in 1895 was $1,322,694. The last curving bar is red for the year 1899 and indicates that the value of household and kitchen furniture owned by Black Georgians reached $1,434,975. Each curving bar grows a bit longer than the previous bar, demonstrating the increasing value of furniture Black Georgians owned in the twenty-five years leading up to the Paris Exposition.

0510.altText: Beginning as a green horizontal bar that branches downward, first to the left in blue and then to the right in yellow, this bar chart ends in a red spiral to indicate where Black inhabitants reside across the country in differently populated regions.
0510.altTextLong: This visualization takes attributes from various chart styles to create a new form of graphing evidence for the Black population in Georgia in 1890. Beginning as a horizontal bar graph near the top of the page, a green bar indicates that there are 78,139 Black inhabitants of Georgian cities in cities whose population exceeds 10,000 people. Branching downward to the left, a small blue bar indicates 8,025 Black inhabitants live in cities whose populations are between 5,000 and 10,000 people. A longer bar branches off from the blue bar downward and to the right in a yellow color, indicating 37,699 Black inhabitants in cities whose population is between 2,500 and 5,000 people. The yellow bar connects to a red bar which spirals downward to the center of the page landing around the number 734,952, which indicates the total Black population in the country and its villages.

0513-db-conjugal.altText: Du Bois and his students’ chart of the conjugal condition. Because of its near symmetry and vibrancy, the graphic resembles a silhouetted image of a city at sunset or a church’s steeple.
0513-db-conjugal.altTextLong: Part grid and part area chart, this colorful graphic shows the marital status of Black men and women in the United States according to their age. The horizontal X axis measures the percentage (from 0 to 100%) of men and women who are single, married, or widowed, and the vertical Y axis measures age. The age increments from bottom to top, are listed as follows: 0 to 15; 15 to 20; 20 to 25; 25 to 30; 30 to 35; 35 to 45; 45 to 55; 55 to 65; and over age 65. Divided vertically in the middle, the left side of the grid tracks Black men’s marital status, and the right side measures Black women’s. Green space, which indicates widowers, occupies each top corner and falls vertically, serving as a border to the majority of the other categories; red space sits next to the green to show who is married; and blue lies in the center and along the bottom next to the red area to depict those who are single. Because of its near symmetry and vibrancy, the graphic looks like an abstract image of a city at sunset, with the central blue area resembling a silhouetted large building, and the red and green areas on either side of the blue depicting the sky.

0515-916-amalg.altText: A chart showing the increasing number of Black and Black multiracial residents in the United States from 1800 to 1890. Drawn resembling a steep mountaintop, the chart’s downward motion emphasizes the range and scope of blackness.
0515-916-amalg.altTextLong: A chart that shows the increasing number of Black and Black multiracial residents in the United States from 1800 to 1890. Drawn resembling a steep mountaintop, which begins at 1800 on the right of the page and falls to 1890 at the bottom left, the chart’s downward motion emphasizes how the range and scope of blackness shifted during the nineteenth century. To depict what Du Bois labels as the “amalgamation” of the growing number of Black people in the United States and their shifting phenotypes, the chart sections off three discrete racial categories by hue, which lighten gradually from black to white. The Black population is colored in black and implies that this portion of the population showed no visual trace of interracial coupling. To its right, the color grows slightly lighter as it nears what Du Bois labels as the “mulatto” or multiracial population, which is split between a light brown and a dark yellow color to depict the portion of the Black population that announces a white presence in one’s lineage. The white population section is predominately drawn with the paper’s off-white hue, except for a light yellow gradient where it comes into contact with the multiracial population, to its left. There is no quantitative data associated with the white population. While no percentages or numbers are stated in the slimmer sections tracking the 1800s or 1840s, the chart shows that by 1860 the Black population amounted to 3,542,147 people–90% of all Black people in America–and the multiracial population made up the remaining 10% of the total Black population. In 1890, while both grew in size, the Black population decreased to 85% (6,337,980 people) while the Black multiracial population increased to 15% (1,113,063 people).

0520a.altText: Two bar diagrams (Du Bois’s original at left, Chalabi’s re-creation at right) of interweaving bars that tracks decreasing illiteracy percentages of Black Georgians. The re-creation adds 2010 statistics to show a significant shift to 2 percent illiteracy.
0520a.altTextLong: A bar diagram of interweaving perpendicular and parallel bars that tracks illiteracy percentages of Black Georgians between 1860 and 1900 every ten years. Each year is listed from earliest to latest, top to bottom, and is connected to its corresponding illiteracy percentage by a bar that, when horizontal, is not shaded in and, when vertical, is colored in black. The four bars begin horizontally and turn downward to connect to their respective percentages, creating a criss-cross pattern. The first bar for the year 1860 measures 99 percent illiteracy in the Black Georgian population, so the horizontal portion of the bar does not extend far into the page. The bar for 1870 measures 92 percent illiteracy, thus the horizontal bar stretches farther than the previous year, but not by much. In 1880, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 81.8 percent, and in 1890, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 67.2 percent, both horizontal bars taking up more space than the previous year(s). Lastly, in 1900, the percentage of illiterate Black Georgians decreased once again to 50 percent of the population, the horizontal bar stretching the width of the chart.

0527-899-series.caption: The title image of the second set of charts prepared for the Paris Exposition, A Series of Statistical Charts Illustrating the Condition of the Descendants of Former African Slaves Now Resident in the United States of America. 0527-899-series.altText: A spread with the university’s mission statement “to raise and civilize the songs of the freedmen by training their more capable members in the liberal arts according to the best standards of the day” next to students’ roles in creating the graphics.
0527-899-series.altTextLong: The first chart in the second series presented at the Paris Exposition is dense with text in both English and French to highlight the history and role of Atlanta University students–and the institution itself–in creating the data portraits. The text describes the year the college was founded (1867), the total number of Black students who have attended the university (6,000 at the time of the study), and the total number of graduates from the university (330 students) who have since gone on to work in various fields described in a pie chart. The multicolor pie chart sits in the middle of the page describing employment and other conditions of Black Americans with a key in English to the left and in French to the right of the chart. The largest section of the pie chart is colored in red and records that 58.5 percent of the Black American population works as teachers. The second largest portion of the chart is yellow and shows 28.1 percent of the population is designated as house wives. Decreasing substantially in size to 4.3 percent is the next population of Black American employees who work as ministers, indicated in blue. Other professions and government service follow at 3.8 and 3.2 percent respectively, with other professions colored in green and government service in pink. The smallest portion of Black American employment is under the category of business, which is shaded in light brown and is recorded at 2.1 percent. A small multicolored map of the United States also rests under the title of the piece with a star over Atlanta, GA to indicate the center of the Black population in the country. More text at the bottom of the page states the number of current Black professors, faculty, and students at Atlanta University at the time of the study (20 professors and faculty; 250 students), along with a description of the size of the campus (60 acres) and number of buildings (5), including the library which holds 11,000 volumes. Lastly, the text describes the university’s endowment of $500,000 and the mission of the university, which is “to raise and civilize the songs of the freedmen by training their more capable members in the liberal arts according to the best standards of the day.”

876.altTextLong: A bar diagram of interweaving perpendicular and parallel bars that tracks illiteracy percentages of Black Georgians between 1860 and 1900 every ten years. Each year is listed from earliest to latest, top to bottom, and is connected to its corresponding illiteracy percentage by a bar that, when horizontal, is not shaded in and, when vertical, is colored in black. The four bars begin horizontally and turn downward to connect to their respective percentages, creating a criss-cross pattern. The first bar for the year 1860 measures 99 percent illiteracy in the Black Georgian population, so the horizontal portion of the bar does not extend far into the page. The bar for 1870 measures 92 percent illiteracy, thus the horizontal bar stretches farther than the previous year, but not by much. In 1880, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 81.8 percent, and in 1890, the illiteracy percentage decreased to 67.2 percent, both horizontal bars taking up more space than the previous year(s). Lastly, in 1900, the percentage of illiterate Black Georgians decreased once again to 50 percent of the population, the horizontal bar stretching the width of the chart.

883.caption: Valuation of town and city property owned by Georgia Negroes. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33883.
883.altTextLong: A line graph overlaid on a red grid of squares measuring the value of Black-owned property in Georgia from 1870 to 1900. The vertical Y axis tracks monetary value by the million dollar, and the horizontal X axis measures the year, where every grid box along the X axis is one year. The line moves diagonally up to the right with peaks in 1872 and 1883 (measured around 1 million and 5 million dollars respectively) before slight dips in monetary value. Between 1879 and 1883, the value of Black-owned property in Georgia increased from just above one million dollars to nearly five million. Dispersed around the line are descriptions of the political atmosphere of the time. For instance, between 1870 and 1872, Du Bois and his affiliates wrote vertically, parallel to the increase in property value, “Ku-Kluxism,” indicating the rise of the Ku Klux Klan. Above the line around the 2.5 million dollar mark before the subsequent decade of the 1880s, another descriptor reads “Political Unrest.” Below the line between the years 1890 and 1895 and below the two million dollar mark, one descriptor is written vertically that says, “Financial panic,” and another above the latter is written horizontally: “Lynching.” The last description on the grid mirrors the “Political Unrest” label on the other side of the line, which reads: “Disenfranchisement and Proscriptive Laws.”

884.altTextLong: A nested circle chart resembling a bull’s-eye that shows the valuation of all taxable Black-owned property in Georgia between the years 1875-1900. The innermost circle is black with white numbering that shows, in 1875, the valuation of taxable Black-owned Georgian property was $5,393,885. The ring surrounding the black circle is brown and shows the valuation of taxable Black-owned property in 1880 was $5,764,293. The next outermost ring is thicker and blue, indicating an increase in taxable property in 1885 to $8,153,390. An even thicker yellow ring surrounds the blue, showing $12,322,003 in 1890. The second outermost ring is smaller and gray and indicates the valuation in 1895 to be $12,941,230. The final outermost circle is red, similarly thin, and shows that the valuation of all taxable Black-owned property in Georgia in 1899 reached $13,447,423. The circle chart is drawn so that each ring has a protruding triangle or point that reaches inward to the 1870 black center. With each overlapping circle, the intrusive triangles become thicker and are overlaid by the other rings’s colors, creating a hypnotic effect as if each circle is being torn back to reveal the black center, emphasized by each triangle’s jagged edges.

893.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33893.
893.caption: Income and expenditure of 150 Negro families in Atlanta, Ga., U.S.A. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33893.
893.altTextLong: A mixed media chart that indicates how Black Georgian families from various class backgrounds make and spend their money. The visualization combines inked typography, photograph, colored charts, mechanical type, and a gold-plated seal of one American dollar. Organized vertically into categories based on family income, the subcategories along the horizontal X axis top the chart to list the cost of rent, food, clothing, taxes, and other expenses and savings. These categories connect to a bar chart that shows the percentage of how much the various classes of Black families spend on each expense. Each expense includes a brief explanatory note or image below it to provide detail about what the percentages refer to. For instance, under “rent,” there is a photograph of a four houses lined up on a street that Du Bois’ team labels a “well-to-do neighborhood.” Similarly, under “clothes,” two portraits of a young Black boy and a Black woman are present. The other three expenses include worded descriptions, like the “other expenses and savings” category, which lists what the team terms “the higher life,” including items like religion, art, amusements, books, and travel. Under each expense description or image, a bar of black, purple, pink, blue, or gray lies to help indicate the percentages of expenses given to each category in the chart. Every income bracket except for the last is paired with the one above it, where those families bringing in $139.10-$249.45 yearly are classified as “poor,” those making $335.86-$433.82 are deemed “fair,” those making $547-$880 are “comfortable,” and finally, the last separate category, those who make $1,125 yearly are “well-to-do.”

899.title: A series of statistical charts illustrating the condition of the descendants of former African slaves now in residence in the United States of America
899.cleanTitle: A series of statistical charts illustrating the condition of the descendants of former African slaves now in residence in the United States of America
899.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-08994.
899.caption: A series of statistical charts illustrating the condition of the descendants of former African slaves now in residence in the United States of America. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-08994.
899.altTextLong: The first chart in the second series presented at the Paris Exposition is dense with text in both English and French to highlight the history and role of Atlanta University students–and the institution itself–in creating the data portraits. The text describes the year the college was founded (1867), the total number of Black students who have attended the university (6,000 at the time of the study), and the total number of graduates from the university (330 students) who have since gone on to work in various fields described in a pie chart. The multicolor pie chart sits in the middle of the page describing employment and other conditions of Black Americans with a key in English to the left and in French to the right of the chart. The largest section of the pie chart is colored in red and records that 58.5 percent of the Black American population works as teachers. The second largest portion of the chart is yellow and shows 28.1 percent of the population is designated as house wives. Decreasing substantially in size to 4.3 percent is the next population of Black American employees who work as ministers, indicated in blue. Other professions and government service follow at 3.8 and 3.2 percent respectively, with other professions colored in green and government service in pink. The smallest portion of Black American employment is under the category of business, which is shaded in light brown and is recorded at 2.1 percent. A small multicolored map of the United States also rests under the title of the piece with a star over Atlanta, GA to indicate the center of the Black population in the country. More text at the bottom of the page states the number of current Black professors, faculty, and students at Atlanta University at the time of the study (20 professors and faculty; 250 students), along with a description of the size of the campus (60 acres) and number of buildings (5), including the library which holds 11,000 volumes. Lastly, the text describes the university’s endowment of $500,000 and the mission of the university, which is “to raise and civilize the songs of the freedmen by training their more capable members in the liberal arts according to the best standards of the day.”

900.altTextLong: A map of the United States displaying a color-coded distribution of Black inhabitants across the nation. Under the title and its French translation, a key showing five circles of colors indicates increasing population density in the following order: the color yellow represents less than one Black resident per square mile, blue represents between one and four Black inhabitants per square mile, red represents between four and eight residents per square mile, brown represents between eight and fifteen inhabitants per square mile, and the color black indicates between fifteen and twenty-five Black residents per square mile. The majority of the west side of the country is yellow, whereas Texas and several midwestern states are shaded blue. Southeastern states are primarily colored as brown, except for South Carolina and Mississippi, which are black. There are infrequent spots of no coloring at all–right above Texas where Oklahoma and Arkansas meet, as well as off the coast of New York, both of which occur nearby red, yellow, and blue shading rather than brown or black.

The Black population is represented by a red line, which remains far below the green line representing the white population. Between 1790 and 1890, the difference in population between the two racial groups grew exponentially; both the white and Black populations began in 1790 under the five million mark and rose to more than fifty million people (white) versus merely seven million (Black) by 1890. The chart also depicts various international and national events in a fainter text across the graph, like the “suppression of slave trade” in 1810, “European immigration” placed between 1840 and 1850, and “Emancipation” between 1860 and 1870, in slightly larger lettering than the previous events. The key on the graph, aside from describing how each population corresponds to the two line colors, notes that the small numbers which lie above the two lines indicate the percentage increase per decade of each population. The page also shows wear along the right edge due to damage, caused either by fire or water.

905.altTextLong: A graphic of three vertical bars that compares various professions Black Georgians engaged in according to their sex. The three bars are each divided into five colors: from top to bottom, the red fragment of the bars represents those who work in agriculture, mining and fishing; blue represents those who work in the vague category of “professions''; yellow shows the amount of Black Georgians who work in domestic and personal service; brown shows commerce and ground transportation; and the bottom fragment of each bar is green, representing manufacturing and mechanical industries. To the left of the bars, each category is described in English, and to the right, the occupations are written in French. 914.altTextLong: A horizontal bar chart comparing the percentage of the Black population who lived in cities and rural areas in America’s former slave states every ten years from 1860 to 1890. The key explains that the red portion of each bar indicates the percentage of the Black population that lived in cities (where the population reached or exceeded 8,000 people), and the black portion of each bar shows the percentage of the Black population who lived in villages or country districts. The Black rural population significantly outweighs the Black presence in cities throughout the forty year period: in 1860, 95.8% of Black Americans resided in rural areas compared to 4.2% who lived in cities in the former slave states. The city population grew marginally in ten years, but shifted only by a tenth of a percent between 1870 and 1880–from 8.5% to 8.4% respectively. The last bar shows that the percentage of Black Americans who lived in cities reached 12% in 1890, indicating that 88% still resided in villages or country districts in the former slave states.

916.title: The Amalgamation of the White and Black elements of the population in the United States.
916.cleanTitle: The Amalgamation of the White and Black elements of the population in the United States.
916.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33916.
916.caption: The Amalgamation of the White and Black elements of the population in the United States. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33916.
916.altTextLong: A chart that shows the increasing number of Black and Black multiracial residents in the United States from 1800 to 1890. Drawn resembling a steep mountaintop, which begins at 1800 on the right of the page and falls to 1890 at the bottom left, the chart’s downward motion emphasizes how the range and scope of blackness shifted during the nineteenth century. To depict what Du Bois labels as the “amalgamation” of the growing number of Black people in the United States and their shifting phenotypes, the chart sections off three discrete racial categories by hue, which lighten gradually from black to white. The Black population is colored in black and implies that this portion of the population showed no visual trace of interracial coupling. To its right, the color grows slightly lighter as it nears what Du Bois labels as the “mulatto” or multiracial population, which is split between a light brown and a dark yellow color to depict the portion of the Black population that announces a white presence in one’s lineage. The white population section is predominately drawn with the paper’s off-white hue, except for a light yellow gradient where it comes into contact with the multiracial population, to its left. There is no quantitative data associated with the white population. While no percentages or numbers are stated in the slimmer sections tracking the 1800s or 1840s, the chart shows that by 1860 the Black population amounted to 3,542,147 people–90% of all Black people in America–and the multiracial population made up the remaining 10% of the total Black population. In 1890, while both grew in size, the Black population decreased to 85% (6,337,980 people) while the Black multiracial population increased to 15% (1,113,063 people).

917.altTextLong: A rectangular graphic separated into four triangles converging at the center detailing the black-owned property value of three states–Georgia, Virginia, and North Carolina–and the total value of all states. The top brown triangle depicts the black-owned property value in Virginia in 1895, which amounted to $13,933,998. The triangle to the left is red and shows that black-owned property value in North Carolina in 1891 totaled $8,018,446. The blue triangle on the right shows that black-owned Georgia property in 1895 was $12,941,230. The bottom triangle is black and depicts the total black-owned property value of all three states in both dollar amount and francs: $34,893,684, or 180,796,290 francs. Because the vertical length of the rectangle graphic is larger than the horizontal width, each rectangle is not proportional to its corresponding property value in relation to the others. For instance, North Carolina and Georgia point towards each other as the triangles on the left and right of the rectangle, but their totals have a difference of over 4 million dollars, even though their triangle dimensions are equal. The same goes for Virginia and the total amount of all three states combined, where Virginia’s brown triangle and the black triangle showing the total of the three point towards each other and have the same dimensions, but have a difference of over 20 million dollars in the black-owned property values they depict.

From top to bottom, the states and their respective percentages of Black landowners are as follows: Virginia, 27% landowners; South Carolina, 18% landowners; Texas, 22% landowners; North Carolina, 19% landowners; Georgia, 12% landowners; Mississippi, 13% landowners; Tennessee, 20% landowners; Louisiana, 125 landowners; Arkansas, 21% landowners.

919.title: Negro business men in the United States.
919.cleanTitle: Negro business men in the United States.
919.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
919.caption: Negro business men in the United States. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
919.altTextLong: A graphic of differently sized and colored squares, which looks less like a chart and more like an abstract geometric painting, alludes to the varying amounts of Black men who worked in different occupations. The estimated capital of each combined job is listed on the top of the chart as $8,784,637 or 45,518,254 francs. Each square is connected to a thin line of the same color to where the title of the occupation is listed vertically on the left side of the page, in English and with a French translation underneath. The first category of work relates to those who worked in general merchandise stories, connected to a wide green rectangle that is the second-largest shape on the page. Underneath it is a large yellow rectangle that is as wide as the green one but much longer, depicting the amount of Black men who worked as grocers. Next is a small red square–the smallest shape of the graphic–that stands in for the amount of men who worked as bankers. A larger blue rectangle, about half the size of the green rectangle for those who worked in general merchandise stores, follows the small red square to depict the amount of men who worked as undertakers. A wide black rectangle falls underneath the blue rectangle to represent men who worked as building contractors. The next occupation is listed as “druggists,” and a brown line runs underneath the black rectangle and down below the yellow grocers shape to connect to a brown square, smaller than the blue above, depicting the amount of men who worked as pharmacists. A large green square of similar dimensions as the blue building contractors shape follows to represent the amount of Black men who worked as publishers. Lastly, a red line stretches underneath the green square and connects to a wide red rectangle, about twice the size of the other small red square, that depicts the amount of men who served as building and loan associates.

920.title: Pauperism among American Negroes.
920.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
920.caption: Pauperism among American Negroes. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
920.altTextLong: Part circle chart and part bar chart, this graphic shows the amount of Black men and women who are poor or “paupers” compared to those who are not. A large brown semicircle takes up the bulk of the page to describe, as the chart says under the title, the “proportion of almshouse paupers in every 100,000 negroes.” Along the bottom edge of the large brown semicircle, which represents 100,000 Black people, a small red semicircle appears, depicting 86 paupers. From the red semicircle, a bar graph is drawn below to show the ratio of Black men–colored in green–compared to women–colored in yellow–who made up those 86 individuals. The green section stretches slightly farther than the yellow, indicating more men than women of those 86 people were in almshouses.

922.title: Crime among American Negroes.
922.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
922.caption: Crime among American Negroes. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
922.altTextLong: A long rectangle, displayed at a forty-five degree angle, is divided into five color blocks to show the various crimes 3,250 Black prisoners committed. The first category listed, corresponding to the topmost sliver of the rectangle, is red to describe crimes against the government. This red slice is the smallest of the graphic. Crimes against society are listed next and colored in yellow, a substantially larger block than the red. Larger still is the next block, colored in brown, to depict crimes against individual persons. The largest block of the rectangle is next and colored in black, nearly twice the size of the brown block, to show crimes Black people committed against property. The final category is colored in green and represents miscellaneous crimes, which is slightly smaller than the yellow category for crimes against society.

923.title: American Negro newspapers and periodicals.
923.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33923.
923.caption: American Negro newspapers and periodicals. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33923.
923.altTextLong: A multicolored pyramid that depicts the various types of writing formats in which Black people published. The tip of the pyramid is a small blue triangle, representing 3 magazines that were published. The following quadrangle is similarly small and colored in red, representing 3 daily papers that were published. The next shape is yellow and slightly larger, showing that 11 school papers were created and distributed. The next section is blue again and takes up nearly half of the pyramid, depicting that 136 weekly papers in total were published and distributed by Black publishers. The last segment of the pyramid is brown and shows the total of all Black publishing efforts, which amounted to 153 newspapers or periodicals.

924.title: Religion of American Negroes.
924.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
924.caption: Religion of American Negroes. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
924.altTextLong: A bar chart showing the Christian religious affiliations of Black people in the United States. The top two categories stretch to twice the height of the remaining bars, showing the number of Catholics compared to Protestants, which are depicted in red and green, respectively. Though pronounced due to its color, the red bar is merely a sliver, showing 14,517 Catholics, while the green bar runs the width of the paper and curls up and over twice, like a blocky spiral, to indicate the vast number of people who were Protestants in comparison, which amounted to 2,659,460 people. Five yellow bars of smaller height follow the red and green to represent the amount of Black people within the different Protestant sects. No concrete numbers are attached to these yellow bars, and length is relied upon to imply comparative amounts. The topmost yellow bar for Baptists stretches the entire width of the page, and the second yellow bar for Methodists reaches just short of the page’s width. The last three yellow bars–depicting Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and those of miscellaneous affiliation, in that order–are strikingly shorter. The bar for Congregationalists is only a slice of yellow, barely perceptible, while the bars for Presbyterians and miscellaneous are small squares of yellow.

925.title: Statistics of Negro church organizations.
925.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
925.caption: Statistics of Negro church organizations. Image courtesy of the Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsca-33865.
925.altTextLong: A spare bar chart of various statistics relating to Black religious organizing. The topmost bar stretches most of the page’s width to show the 23,462 church organizations in the country. The second bar depicts the number of church edifices, which runs the entire width of the page and comes to 23,770 buildings. The next statistic is a monetary amount rather than a bar, set in a bold font, to claim the total value of these church properties, which is written as $26,626,448 or 137,960,860 francs. The last bar at the bottom of the page, which runs the entire width of the page, represents the 2,673,977 communicants who run, organize, and attend these religious events. For reference, underneath the communicants bar, a smaller bar shows the population of New York in comparison, which reaches about three-fourths of the length depicting Black communicants.
